items.title: onedevatlas is open: one connected graph for SAP developers
items.author: mike_zaschka
items.text:
Today onedevatlas opens to everyone. It is one connected graph of what is built for SAP development, by SAP and by everyone else: packages, plugins, services, tools, MCP servers and skills, the problems they answer, the posts and talks that explain them, and the people who make them. One graph, read by people and by their agents. 

 Why it exists 
 Building has never been easier, and being found has never been harder. On 3 October the atlas listed 31 MCP servers for ABAP. Today it lists 42. Most of them are careful work, and many solve the same problem, because their makers could not see what was already there. Agents make it sharper: an agent knows what it was trained on and what the skills beside it describe, and the work of a freelancer, a partner or a customer team is rarely part of its answer. 
 The lists we have, for CAP, for UI5, for ABAP, are good and separate. What was missing is a view across the stacks, with SAP's work and the community's side by side, and a graph underneath that says how things relate. 

 A map drawn by capability 
 Every door, CAP, UI5, ABAP and BTP, and the smaller ones for SAP Commerce, SAP SuccessFactors and SAP Digital Manufacturing, has its own map. One hexagon is one capability, a concern a project has, and its colour says who is present: SAP, the community, both, or nobody yet. Open a tile and the capability page says what SAP ships, where that stops, and who else is present. Under a capability, use cases make the options comparable by the outcome they cover and the conditions under which they cover it, never by stars or downloads. 
 Behind the map is the graph itself, at /graph : select a node and its card says what it provides, who maintains it and what it depends on, each edge with one meaning. 
 The same answers for your agent 
 The hosted MCP server at https://onedevatlas.dev/mcp answers with the same facts the pages show. This exchange was recorded against the live server today: a question about letting a coding agent change ABAP in an on-premise system lands on a capability, then on an assessed use case with seven options, six covering it under conditions and one not known, and the four things that decide between them for your system. 
 Explore, and TechEd week 
 The third way in is a flight. Explore and Play is the same graph as a place: make an orb, design a ship and fly through the ecosystems. Until Sunday 1 November, midnight in Berlin, it is shared: sign in with GitHub, meet other pilots, play rock, paper, scissors (SAP style) and collect points for what you look at. Then the boards freeze, and the leaders stay in the atlas's history. 

 Take part 
 If your work is missing or something about it is wrong, open an issue . Anything about a person goes directly through the contact form. Maintainers can sign in and write a note on their own entry. 
 The full article explains the words the atlas uses and how to read a capability page, and its discussion is open. 
 See you at TechEd, or in flight. 🚀

items.title: What’s New in Identity and Access Management in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
items.author: SafaBahoosh
items.text:
1. Overview 
 Identity and Access Management (IAM) in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition provides the foundational security layer that controls user access to business applications and backend services. Traditionally, IAM apps were grouped into business catalogs, with authorization default values aggregated strictly at the catalog level. These business catalogs served as the essential building blocks for constructing business roles. The traditional authorization flow works as follows: 
 Business Role → Business Catalog → Fiori→ Authorization Defaults / Services 
 While this catalog-centric model provided a straightforward way to bundle related apps, it operated on an "all-or-nothing" principle. Assigning a catalog granted access to every application within it. 
 To solve these limitations, SAP evolved the IAM architecture from rigid catalog bundles to modular application entities. 

 2. What Is "App as Entity"? 
 Starting with Release 2502, SAP introduced “App Authorization Variants” for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. An App Authorization Variant acts as a standalone wrapper around an application's authorization requirements, decoupling it from the catalog to make the individual IAM App -rather than the catalog- the smallest assignable unit of authorization. 
 With Release 2608, this capability expands into the broader "App as Entity" framework, enabling administrators to directly assign, toggle active/inactive, and manage application access with fine-grained precision when building Business Roles. 
 The diagram below illustrates this shift from broad catalog bundling to standalone, app-level role construction. 

 2.1 The Challenges of the Catalog-Only Approach 
 While catalogs provide great pre-bundled workplaces, relying solely on them introduced friction: 
 Inability to create business roles for a specific subset of apps without custom catalog creation. 
 High change-management effort when catalogs required splitting due to evolving requirements. 
 Automatic exposure of newly added apps to end-users upon upgrades, along with their underlying authorizations. 
 By shifting to "App as Entity," administrators can now assemble roles based on exact user tasks without rigid constraints, enabling the direct launch of all application types via assigned transaction codes in S/4HANA Public Edition and SAP BTP, ABAP environment. 
 2.2 Practical Scenarios: 
 User Management: Grant user access to the Business User app without exposing access to the Business Roles app. 
 Procurement: Assign access to a specific Purchase Order app without granting permissions to all applications inside the broader Procurement catalog. 

 3. How App Assignment Works 
 "App as Entity" does not replace Business Catalogs. Instead, Business Catalogs and direct app selection run side-by-side in parallel. 
 When configuring a role in the Maintain Business Roles Fiori app (F1492), administrators now have two assignment mechanisms: 

 Assignment Type 
 How It Works 
 Best Used For 

 Assigned via Business Catalog 
 The Business Catalog is assigned to the Business Role. IAM Apps within that catalog can be selectively activated or deactivated and are part of the resulting role accordingly. 
 Standard role setup where a user needs the complete suite of applications in a functional area. 

 Direct Assignment 
 An App Authorization Variant /IAM App is selected directly for a Business Role without requiring the overarching Business Catalog to be assigned. 
 Granular role setup where a user needs only 1 or 2 specific applications from a larger domain. 
 3.1 In-App Granular Control 
 Beyond assigning broad Business Catalogs, administrators can now manage application access with pinpoint accuracy. The Maintain Business Roles app (F1492) allows security leads to directly add, remove, toggle, or inspect individual IAM Apps to match exact user job responsibilities. 
 3.1.1 Practical Example: Direct App Selection in Action 
 To see how "App as Entity" works in practice, consider configuring the "Internal Sales Representative" role as an example inside the Maintain Business Roles app. 

 As shown in the screenshot above, administrators are no longer limited to managing entire catalogs. Instead, the dedicated IAM Apps tab allows granular control over individual applications: 
 Direct App Authorization Variants: Specific apps, such as Display Business Partner , Display Customer (Centrally) , or Supplier are assigned directly as "App Authorization Variants" with their linked transaction objects. 
 Selection & Activation Control: Checkboxes alongside each IAM App let administrators select specific items to Add, Remove, Activate, or Deactivate permissions without affecting the rest of the business domain. 
 Catalog-Free Flexibility: Notice that this role has 0 Business Catalogs assigned yet contains 27 IAM Apps assigned directly. This proves that roles can now be built using standalone app entities tailored to exact job tasks. 
 3.1.2 Toggling Apps ON/OFF 
 In addition to Direct Assignment, administrators can open an assigned Business Catalog inside the Maintain Business Roles app (F1492) and toggle individual IAM Apps ON or OFF. 
 Important Note on Toggling: 
 Toggling an app OFF inside F1492 suppresses its underlying authorization defaults for that specific Business Role instance only. It does NOT alter or remove the app definition from the underlying Business Catalog in ABAP Development Tools (ADT), preserving the central catalog definition for other roles. 

 4. Application Scope: SAP Standard vs. Customer-Developed Apps 
 The "App as Entity" model applies to both SAP-delivered content and custom-built extensions: 
 4.1 SAP Standard Applications 
 As introduced in Section 2, SAP delivers standard content pre-configured as individual App Authorization Variants (SIA6 objects). 
 For standard applications, this eliminates the need to assign full standard catalogs. Security administrators can directly select individual SAP standard apps when building Business Roles, ensuring users receive access only to the exact standard functionality required for their tasks while avoiding the overhead of creating custom catalogs in ADT. 
 4.2 Customer-Developed Applications (Developer Extensibility) 
 Custom applications built via ABAP Cloud / ADT using the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) are defined as External IAM Apps (SIA6 objects). 
 The Migration Requirement: To enable custom apps for individual selection in Business Roles, existing customer IAM Apps (SIA6) and their corresponding Business Catalogs (GBAK objects) must undergo a one-time migration using the built-in migration wizard in ABAP Development Tools (ADT). 
 The Outcome: Once migrated, customer-developed apps can participate in direct assignments and individual toggling just like SAP standard applications. 

 5 On-Premise (PFCG) to Cloud IAM Migration Realities 
 A common question during cloud transformation projects is whether existing On-Premise PFCG roles can be migrated directly into S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. 
 5.1 Key Architectural Differences 

 Feature 
 On-Premise (PFCG) 
 S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (IAM) 

 Primary Building Block 
 Transactions (TCODES), Auth Objects, & Profiles 
 IAM Apps (SIA6), Business Catalogs, & Business Roles 

 Menu Maintenance 
 Direct TCode insertion in PFCG Menu tab 
 IAM Apps bundled in Business Catalogs via ADT 

 Authorization Abstraction 
 Direct maintenance of Auth Objects & Fields in SU24 
 Managed via IAM Apps, Business Catalogs, and Restriction Types 
 5.2 Migration Reality 
 Because On-Premise PFCG roles lack the underlying IAM App metadata layer (SIA6 objects), there is no automated 1-to-1 role import tool. 
 Best Practice: Customers migrating from On-Premise to S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition must construct their business roles using standard SAP reference catalogs or custom IAM Apps created in ADT. 

 6 Key Takeaways 
 Greater Flexibility: Security teams can build roles aligned with real user job descriptions using Direct Assignment or Catalog-based Assignment. 
 Reduced Customization: Eliminates the need to build redundant custom catalogs in ADT just to exclude a single application. 
 Segregation of Duties (SoD) Preserved: Business Catalogs remain the standard for grouping apps and preserving regularly audited SoD compliance. App as Entity adds fine-grained flexibility on top of this foundation . 
 Migration Needed for Custom Content: Existing customer-developed IAM Apps (SIA6) and catalogs (GBAK) must be migrated via the ADT wizard to participate in direct assignment. 

 7 More to read: 
 To dive deeper, explore the following official resources and reference guides: 
 Identity and Access Management (IAM) 
 Maintain Business Roles (Fiori App F1492) 
 Creating an IAM App for the Business Service 
 IAM Information System App (F2450) Usage Guide

items.title: E-learning Available: Driving Finance Transformation by Converting to SAP S/4HANA
items.author: IcyHuang
items.text:
For many organisations running SAP ERP, the journey to SAP S/4HANA represents far more than a technical upgrade - it is a fundamental transformation of the finance function. Legacy ERP finance architectures rely on separate data structures for financial accounting, controlling, and asset accounting, requiring complex reconciliation processes, batch-driven reporting cycles, and significant manual effort during period-end close. These constraints limit real-time financial visibility, slow down decision-making, and create a growing gap between what the business needs and what the finance organization can deliver. 
 Converting to SAP S/4HANA Finance offers the opportunity to fundamentally re-architect how financial data is captured, processed, and reported - unlocking real-time insights, simplifying the data model, and enabling a faster, more intelligent close. To help finance professionals, project team members, and consultants navigate this transformation, this 1.5-hour e-learning course guides learners through the essential finance changes, conversion activities, and data migration steps involved in moving to SAP S/4HANA Finance. 
 What You’ll Learn 
 This e-learning walks through the key finance activities involved in an SAP S/4HANA conversion, from getting your SAP ERP system ready for the move to validating data and completing FI/CO tasks after go-live. Along the way, you'll see practical system checks, real project insights, and guidance to help ensure a smooth and successful conversion. 
 The e-learning course contains below topics with an assessment at the end to test your knowledge. 
 Identify and complete key preparation activities in SAP ERP to ensure readiness for an SAP S/4HANA conversion.

 Apply FI/CO post-conversion responsibilities and best practices using insights and lessons learned from real project experiences.

 Every shipment in SAP Transportation Management needs an owner, someone sells the service, someone buys capacity from a carrier, and someone plans and runs the move. The organizational structure tells the system who those teams are TM fills in the right teams on your orders, sends approvals to the right people, and passes clean data to billing. Get it wrong, and you fight it on every document. I walk through how the org structure works in SAP TM, using a demo company I built called Meridian Cargo Solutions.

items.title: One Plan, Any Level: Customer Hierarchy Planning in SAP Revenue Growth Management
items.author: karenshentu
items.text: Key Account Managers in consumer products companies rarely plan at a single customer level — yet most planning tools still force them to. SAP Revenue Growth Management's Plan at Any Customer Level capability changes this: KAMs can now manage promotion at different customer levels (e.g. national and regional promotions) within one account plan, with level-specific commercial conditions applied automatically and overlapping activities surfaced at the point of planning — not after execution. The result is less time on plan maintenance and execution, and more time on the decisions that drive revenue. Read on to explore how hierarchy-aware planning works in practice — and how you can help shape what comes next.

 I’m working with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and the Spanish SII (received invoices, daily submission), and I’ve run into the following case. I’d appreciate it if anyone who has solved it could share their experience. 
 Scenario: A supplier invoice is posted and submitted to the SII in period A (closed, with the VAT return already filed). Later, the invoice has to be reversed for accounting reasons, and the reversal is posted in period B (open). The invoice is then re-posted correctly in period B. 
 Problem: 
 If the reversal inherits the original tax reporting date, a deregistration request is generated pointing to period A. The customer does not want a filed period to be modified. 
 If I change the tax reporting date of the reversal document to period B, the submission fails with error 3019: “El Ejercicio y Periodo del PeriodoLiquidacion deben coincidir con el último movimiento anterior”. 
 Customer requirement: The correction should be reported in the current period with the opposite sign, without manual intervention in the SII, so that the books match what has been reported. The same process should also work when the reversal falls in the same period as the original invoice. 
 What I have checked: The configuration activity for handling reversal documents (102954) offers the options “Send deregistration or set status cancelled”, “Always send deregistration” and “Send new invoice with type F1/F2/R1/R1S/R2/R2S/R3/R3S”. However, the setting is fixed per company code and document type, so it cannot distinguish between same-period and different-period reversals. 
 Questions: 
 Has anyone encountered error 3019 in this scenario, and how did you solve it? 
 Does sending the reversal as a new invoice (F1/R1) with the current period’s tax reporting date avoid the error in practice? 
 Is there a way for the standard to send a deregistration for same-period reversals and an opposite-sign entry for reversals of closed periods? 
 Thanks in advance.

items.title: Off-Neo migration of HTML5 Applications — Now with AI Skills
items.author: NachshonVagmayster
items.text:
Migrating HTML5 Applications from Neo to Application Frontend Service — Now with AI Skills 
 SAP Neo is approaching end of life , and if you have HTML5 applications hosted there, you already know you need to move them to the multi-cloud environment. Application Frontend service is the natural destination — it brings back the simplicity and flexibility that Neo developers valued, now built on the multi-cloud foundation. 
 While SAP Business Application Studio provides a number of tools to assist with migration, the process is still mostly manual. It can take a few hours for a simple application and up to days for a large-scale application. 
 We are happy to share a set of AI skills we built to automate most of this work. 
 Check out these earlier posts for more background about Application Frontend service: 
 Introducing Application Frontend Service 
 Simple UI Applications with Application Frontend Service 
 Moving HTML5 Applications to Application Frontend Service 
 What Are These AI Skills? 
 The skill focuses is migration from SAP Neo, but it can also migrate applications based on HTML5 Repository that use a managed approuter or standalone approuter. It targets Cloud Foundry or Kyma runtimes and supports both XSUAA and IAS authentication. 
 The package ships with three skills, each covering a different phase of the migration lifecycle: 
 /appfront:migrate analyses your existing HTML5 project, proposes a migration plan, waits for your approval, and then executes all the configuration changes. It never modifies your original project — it copies your original project to a new folder appfront-migrated/ and all changes are done to this copy. 
 /appfront:validate validates your migrated project configuration for correctness and deployment readiness. It goes through mta.yaml, xs-app.json, xs-security.json, and service bindings, and reports any issues against a known-good checklist. It can also connect to a live deployed application and validate it at runtime. 
 /appfront:cleanup is used if you want to completely roll back all changes done with the skill. It un-deploys any deployed applications and any related service instances and removes the local output folder. It always asks before any destructive step and never touches your original source project. 
 The skills are open source and available on GitHub: https://github.com/SAP-samples/html5-applications-migration-skills-for-sap-btp . 
 What Does the Skill Actually Do? 
 When you run /appfront:migrate on a Neo HTML5 project, the skill works through the migration in phases: 
 First, it reads and analyses your source files — neo-app.json, neo-mta.yaml, and manifest.json — and builds a complete picture of your routing, security constraints, and destinations. It then presents you with a migration plan: exactly which files will be created, which will be modified, and which Neo-specific artifacts will be removed. Nothing changes until you approve. 
 Once you confirm, the skill generates the full Application Frontend configuration: 
 xs-app.json — translated your neo-app.json routes and configurations 
 xs-security.json — Neo security constraints mapped to XSUAA scopes, role templates, and role collections 
 mta.yaml — with a content deployer module for deploying the application resources to Application Frontend 
 It also updates manifest.json, fixes the UI5 bootstrap path in index.html, and removes Grunt-based build artifacts that are no longer needed. 
 After generating the files, a built-in critic reviews the output against a checklist to identify common misconfigurations before you deploy. 
 Note: some steps still require manual action in the BTP cockpit — destination credentials with secrets are not exported from Neo for security reasons, so you will need to add those manually after import. 
 How Much Time Does It Save? 
 The table below provides an estimated comparison of the time needed to migrate applications manually and with the help of the AI skills, highlighting the potential time savings for applications of different sizes: 

 App size 
 Manual effort 
 Skill-assisted 
 Time saved 

 Small (1–3 routes, simple roles) 
 ~3 hours 
 ~30 min 
 ~85% 

 Medium (4–10 routes, multiple roles) 
 ~1 day (8 h) 
 ~1.5 hours 
 ~82% 

 Large (10+ routes, complex roles, WorkZone) 
 1–2 days 
 ~4 hours 
 ~75% 
 Note that end-to-end functional testing of your business logic is not included in these estimates. It requires developer or end user involvement and takes the same time regardless of how the technical migration was done. 
 Mass Migration 
 The skills support mass migration of applications. If you have multiple applications with similar characteristics, you can run the skills to migrate all of them in one go. During the process, you can consolidate applications under the same business solution and MTA deployment or keep them completely independent. Simply answer the questions presented by the skill and, if needed, provide instructions in natural language to fine-tune the migration. 
 Prerequisites and How to Get It 
 To use the migration skills, you will need: 
 AI Coding tool like Claude Code installed and connected to an LLM service 
 An SAP BTP subaccount with subscription to Application Frontend service 
 Cloud Foundry CLI installed and logged in to your target org and space 
 MBT (Cloud MTA Build Tool) installed: npm install -g mbt 
 [Optional] Application Frontend CLI (afctl) installed and logged in for fetching the application URL after deployment: npm install -g @SAP /appfront-cli 
 Detailed prerequisite list and installation instructions are available in the README file. The skills were built with Claude Code in mind, but they can be installed and used in other coding tools like GitHub Copilot. 
 Once the skills are installed navigate to your project directory and run /appfront:migrate to get started. 
 To sum up 
 If you still have HTML5 applications running in the SAP Neo environment, now is the time to migrate them to SAP multi-cloud. The good news is that, with AI skills like the ones above, the process has become much easier. 
 Give it a try and let me know in the comments how it worked for you. If you have suggestions for improvement, the best approach would be to contribute them directly to the project’s Git repository.

items.title: Authorization Control in Manage Maintenance Notifications via App Authorization Variants (AAVs)
items.author: Dhriti
items.text:
Manage Maintenance Notifications (F5777) is the next-generation app for the maintenance notification lifecycle consolidating what previously required multiple apps — from creating a maintenance notification to screening, editing, accepting, and creating a maintenance order. 
 The same app is expected to be used by people with different responsibilities during maintenance execution, but not everyone using F5777 should be able to do the same things within it. This is exactly where authorization control can be achieved by App Authorization Variants (AAVs) . 
 This blog focuses on the different App Authorization Variants for Manage Maintenance Notifications (F5777) app and how they can be leveraged for different roles. To know the fundamentals of App Authorization Variants, please refer to these blogs- SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2502: Flexible Business Role Design with App Authorization Variants and Precise Control of Fiori App Access with the App Authorization Variants . 
 The 4 AAVs of Manage Maintenance Notifications (F5777)- 
 Each App Authorization Variant corresponds to a persona and defines what that persona can do inside the app. 

 AAV 
 Persona 
 Key Capability 

 F5777_EMP_TRAN 
 Maintenance Employee or Maintenance Technician 
 Create maintenance notification; edit only on request. 

 F5777_MPL_TRAN 
 Maintenance Planner 
 Employee access along with Assign/Create maintenance orders for notifications. 

 F5777_TRAN 
 Maintenance Supervisor 
 Full notification lifecycle except for Order creation/assignment — create, screen, accept, edit throughout. 

 F5777_EXCP_TRAN 
 Operator 
 Employee access along with creation of Emergency work and Minor work. 
 Let us look at each one. 
 1. F5777_EMP_TRAN | Maintenance Employee | SAP_EAM_BC_MN_MNG_EMP_PC 
 This variant is designed for maintenance employees or maintenance technicians who spot issues and raise them in the system. 
 A user with this AAV can create maintenance notifications and read all notification types. However, their ability to edit is limited. They can only edit a notification when: 
 The notification is moved to an "Action Required" subphase, 
 AND 
 Creator or the User is the or the designated Person Responsible for that notification. 
 This AAV is part of the standard role template SAP_BR_EMPLOYEE_MAINTENANCE , belonging to business catalog SAP_EAM_BC_MN_MNG_EMP_PC . 
 Using the standard role template SAP_BR_EMPLOYEE_MAINTENANCE may enable 'Set Deletion flag' for the user due to additional business authorization coming from other catalogs in the role template. 

 Fig 1: Actions enabled for employee when notification is in Action Required subphase 
 2. F5777_MPL_TRAN | Maintenance Planner | SAP_EAM_BC_MN_MNG_MPL_PC 
 This AAV enables the maintenance planner to create notifications and allows to create or assign maintenance orders for accepted notifications. The Edit authorization is same as in F5777_EMP_TRAN AAV. This variant even allows user to delete and complete the notification. 

 Fig 2: List report view for user with AAV F5777_MPL_TRAN 

 Fig 3: Object page view when notification is created 

 Fig 4: Create and Assign Order enabled for accepted maintenance notification 
 The variant F5777_MPL_TRAN is part of standard role template SAP_BR_MAINTENANCE_PLANNER , belonging to business catalog SAP_EAM_BC_MN_MNG_MPL_PC . 
 This role template gives additional authorizations to the user as compared to the App Authorization Variant F5777_MPL_TRAN such as- Creation of minor/emergency work, accepting, and editing the maintenance notification. 

 Fig 5: Additional actions enabled in standard planner role template for submitted maintenance notification 
 3. F5777_TRAN | Maintenance Supervisor | SAP_EAM_BC_MN_MNG_PC 
 A user assigned with this AAV can work with notifications across all phases — from the moment a notification is raised to when it is completed. They can create, view, screen, accept, reject, and edit maintenance notifications. Editing is not phase-restricted; the supervisor can update a notification whether it is unscreened, in action-required state, or already accepted. The user can’t create or assign maintenance order for accepted notifications with this AAV. 

 Fig 6: Object page view for user with F5777_TRAN AAV when a notification is created 
 This AAV is part of the standard role template SAP_BR_MAINT_SUPERVISOR , belonging to business catalog SAP_EAM_BC_MN_MNG_PC . 
 Unlike the AAV F5777_TRAN, the standard role template SAP_BR_MAINT_SUPERVISOR offers the user to even create or assign maintenance order for accepted notifications due to additional authorizations from other business catalogs in the role template. 

 Fig 7: Additional actions enabled in standard supervisor role template for accepted maintenance notification 
 4. F5777_EXCP_TRAN | SAP_EAM_BC_MN_MNG_PC 
 This variant gives a user maintenance employee-level access combined with an expanded emergency and minor work creation authorization for maintenance notifications — beyond what F5777_EMP_TRAN allows, but without the screening scope of F5777_TRAN. 
 This is the most nuanced of the four, and it exists for a very specific real-world situation – the Operator role . 
 The operator use case, addressed by F5777_EXCP_TRAN, is a good example of the kind of real-world role complexity that AAVs are designed to handle — cleanly, within the standard SAP authorization model. 

 Fig 8: Maintenance employee access extended with create minor and emergency work. 
 Note: The maintenance employee can be restricted to creating either emergency work or minor work along with standard maintenance notification by maintaining restrictions in the role assigned to the user. The restriction should be applied for 'Maintenance Notification Processing Context' to support either of the options-minor or emergency. 

 Fig 9: Restriction applied for Emergency Work (01) 

 Fig 10: User can only create emergency and standard maintenance notifications 
 This is a small example of how a single app can serve very different personas through AAVs — each variant reflecting a specific set of responsibilities without over- or under-provisioning access. 
 You can see AAVs give you more precise control over authorizations, but as an admin, while designing roles, you should also consider what additional dependencies should be added to the role apart from the dependencies already proposed when adding an AAV.

items.title: M&A Engagements: Works Council Engagement - A Gating Item for HR System Migrations
items.author: manubhutani
items.text:
HR TECHNOLOGY M&A INTEGRATION 
 Works Council Engagement: A Gating Item for HR 
 System Migrations 
 Co-determination, consultation, and approval rights over HR systems and employee data 

 Who this is for: program leads, HRIS teams, Legal, and Privacy teams moving an acquired workforce onto a new HR platform (for example from Workday into SAP SuccessFactors) where acquired employees sit in countries with works councils. 
 1. Why this is a gating item 
 Works council engagement is not a lift and shift vs. harmonize choice. In countries with works councils, the council often has legal rights to be informed, consulted, or to approve a new HR system before employee data can move. Missing this can delay go-live regardless of how ready the technology is. 

 The core message 
 A system can be fully configured, tested, and signed off by the business, and still be blocked at the last step. Treat works council approval as a formal go-live readiness criterion, owned and tracked like any other critical-path item. 

 What is at stake if it is skipped 

 Country example 
 Possible consequence of proceeding without the required process 

 Germany 
 The council can seek injunctive relief to stop use of a monitoring-capable system until co-determination is respected, and the matter can end up before a conciliation committee. 

 Netherlands 
 A decision taken without required consent can be declared void if the council invokes this in time, and the council can contest the decision. 

 France 
 Courts have ordered deployments of new tools suspended until the information and consultation procedure is completed, in some cases with daily penalties. 

 All countries 
 Delayed go-live, loss of trust with the workforce, rework of design decisions, and reputational and legal exposure. 

 2. Understand the rights you are dealing with 
 Not every council right is the same. The strength of the right changes what you must prepare and how long the process can take. In practice, three levels matter. 
 The spectrum of works council rights 

 INFORM 
 → 
 CONSULT 
 → 
 CONSENT 

 Council receives the facts 
 before decisions are final 

 Council gives an opinion 
 and the employer must hear it 
 before deciding 

 No lawful rollout without 
 agreement, or a substitute 
 ruling or conciliation 

 Typical for: early information on planned technical systems (for example Germany, Sec. 90 BetrVG) 

 Typical for: France, where the CSE is informed and consulted on new technology and on tools that monitor activity 

 Typical for: Germany (Sec. 87 BetrVG) and the Netherlands (Art. 27 WOR) for systems that can monitor or that process personnel data 
 Rights differ by country and by what the system does. Always confirm with local counsel. 

 Why HR systems usually trigger these rights 
 An HR platform holds personnel data, and rules about processing and protecting that data are often subject to council rights. 
 Several statutes look at capability, not intent. A system that can observe or record behavior or performance can trigger consent rights even if the employer promises not to use it that way. 
 Talent modules go further. Performance, goals, and assessment criteria are frequently treated as evaluation schemes, which have their own consent or consultation rules. 
 Analytics, dashboards, and AI-assisted features can widen the scope. Switching a feature on later can reopen the discussion. 

 How the level shapes your plan 

 Level 
 What it means for the program 
 Plan for 

 Inform 
 No veto, but early notice builds trust and avoids disputes later 
 • Brief the council early 
 • Share a dossier summary and a named contact 

 Consult 
 The council's opinion must be heard before the decision is taken, so timing matters 
 • Allow a real review period 
 • Document how feedback was handled 
 • Decide only after consultation closes 

 Consent 
 The council can withhold agreement, which may lead to negotiation, conciliation, or a court route 
 • Treat as critical path 
 • Negotiate a written agreement 
 • Prepare a contingency per country 

 3. What works councils typically focus on 
 Councils generally ask the same core questions, even when the legal basis differs. Preparing a clear answer to each, in writing and in the local language, is the single most effective way to shorten the process. 

 Topic 
 What the council asks 
 What to bring 

 Data 
 What employee data is collected, what moves to the new system, and why it is needed 
 • Field-level data inventory: field, source, target, purpose 
 • Rationale for each category, and what is not migrated 

 Data security 
 Where data is hosted, how it is protected, and who else can touch it 
 • Hosting location, encryption, cross-border transfer mechanism 
 • Vendor and sub-processor list with access scope 

 Data access 
 Who can see what, and how sensitive fields are protected 
 • Role and permission matrix (managers, HR, support, offshore teams) 
 • Live demo of what each role sees, including sensitive fields 

 Historical data 
 What is retained, what is archived, and how people can reach their records 
 • Retention schedule and archive location 
 • Process for current and former employees to request records 

 Monitoring 
 Assurance that the system will not be used to watch individuals 
 • Written statement of purposes and prohibited uses 
 • Status of analytics and AI features (on, off, planned) 

 Language 
 Whether employees can understand and use the system 
 • Translated job aids, notices, and training 
 • Known language gaps and the mitigation 

 Employee rights 
 How access, correction, and deletion requests are handled 
 • GDPR rights process and contacts 
 • Employee notice and communication plan 

 Tip: share the data model, not the data 
 The inventory should describe data elements and purposes, not individual employee records. Disclosing personal data to the council can itself need a legal basis, so keep examples anonymized or in test data. 

 4. A practical engagement approach 
 Run the works council track as its own workstream with an owner, a plan, and a status line in the program dashboard. A five-phase approach keeps Legal, Privacy, HR, and the program team aligned. 
 Five phases of works council engagement 

 1 Scope 
 2 Prepare 
 3 Brief and demo 
 4 Agree 
 5 Sustain 

 • Identify entities and countries 
 • Confirm council exists and level (local or central) 
 • Agree owners and timeline 
 • Align Legal, Privacy, HR on one answer set 
 • Translate key materials 
 • Early briefing, before design is final 
 • Live demos of security and access 
 • Log questions and commitments 
 • Negotiate works agreement or opinion 
 • Resolve open points in writing 
 • Obtain formal approval or consultation close 
 • Track as go-live criterion 
 • Re-open if scope changes 
 • Keep a named contact post go-live 

 Best practices 
 Engage early, before design is final. Councils want to shape decisions, not rubber-stamp them. 
 Bring a field-level data inventory showing what is migrated and why. 
 Run live demos of the actual security model, role access, and what managers can see. 
 Give one set of answers. Align Legal, Privacy, and local HR, and document commitments in a works agreement where required. 
 Plan for their cycle. Build review cycles (weeks to months) into the plan, provide translated materials and a named contact, and track approval as a formal go-live readiness criterion.

items.title: Transition to SuccessFactors from non SAP system in an M&A engagement
items.author: manubhutani
items.text:
Transition to SuccessFactors from non SAP system in an M&A engagement 
 Lift and shift or harmonize? A high-level guide to the critical focus areas 

 Applies when the parent runs on SAP SuccessFactors and acquired company runs on a different HR platform like Workday. 
 Summary 
 When an acquired company runs on a non-SAP HCM platform and the parent runs on SAP SuccessFactors, the integration is rarely a single decision. It is a series of area-by-area choices between two paths: lift and shift the acquired company's way of working or harmonize onto the parent's standards. 
 Two ways to bring an acquired population into the parent system 

 LIFT AND SHIFT 
 HARMONIZE 

 • Keep the acquired structures 
 • Fastest path and lowest Day 1 risk (based upon TSA timeline) 
 • Honors commitments to employees 
 • Creates clean-up work after go-live 
 • Adopt the parent's standards 
 • Unified structure, cleaner analytics 
 • Needs HR and business alignment 
 • Higher change impact for employees on day 1 

 Part A: Foundation Areas 
 These areas define how people, jobs, and organizations are represented in SuccessFactors Employee Central. 
 1. Job Architecture 
 Job codes, job families, levels and grades, job profiles, titles 

 Lift and shift 
 Carry the acquired company's job codes and titles into SuccessFactors as-is, utilizing existing job families and adding new. 

 Harmonize 
 Map all acquired roles into the parent's existing job architecture before load. 

 Focus areas 
 • Mapping Workday job profiles to EC job classifications 
 • Preserving FLSA/exempt status and EEO and other compliance fields 
 • Level calibration, pay range impact, and title changes if harmonizing 
 • Impact on compa-ratio for compensation module 

 Best practice 
 Lift and shift for Day 1 so harmonization can happen later without rework, unless the role mapping is obvious and already approved. 

 2. Organization Structure and Legal Entities 
 Supervisory orgs vs. departments, cost centers, legal entities, positions 

 Lift and shift 
 Recreate the acquired structure as a standalone branch in the parent's org tree. 

 Harmonize 
 Fold teams into the parent's departments, cost centers, and reporting lines. 

 Focus areas 
 • Legal entity and cost center setup (finance and payroll dependencies) 
 • Position management vs. non-position models 
 • Manager hierarchy accuracy and approval chains (OrgLab can be used to define future state reporting structure) 
 • Employees with dotted-line or matrix relationships 

 Best practice 
 Keep a clear structure as much as possible at go-live, then you can align in planned waves based upon finance and legal entity decisions. 

 3. Compensation and Benefits Structures 
 Pay grades, salary ranges, bonus plans, benefit plans, merit cycles 

 Lift and shift 
 Preserve existing pay structures and plan eligibility to honor commitments. 

 Harmonize 
 Move employees to the parent's structures and programs. 

 Focus areas 
 • There may be Legal or contractual obligations to maintain pay and benefits for a defined period 
 • Country-specific compensation plans 
 • Integration with payroll and benefits vendors 
 • Alignment of merit and bonus cycles with the go-live 

 Best practice 
 Cover the existing terms at transition. Harmonization can be done later with job architecture harmonization 

 4. Business Rules and Workflows 
 Approvals, hire/term/transfer rules,event reasons 

 Lift and shift 
 Replicate acquired company processes in SuccessFactors as closely as possible. 

 Harmonize 
 Adopt the parent's standard workflows and rules. 

 Focus areas 
 • Workday business processes do not map one-to-one to SF workflows and business rules 
 • Defaults such as work schedule hours at hire 
 • Termination logic and workflow conditions 
 • Event and reason code alignment 

 Best practice 
 Default to the parent's standard processes. Replicating acquired company logic in SF usually adds complexity at go-live. Make exceptions only for legal or country needs for a successful go-live 

 5. Security and Access (RBP) 
 Role-based permissions, groups, sensitive data, single sign-on 

 Lift and shift 
 Replicate the acquired company's security roles. 

 Harmonize 
 Build access on the parent's role and group model. 

 Focus areas 
 • Rebuild in RBP groups and roles rather than copying Workday/third party security to avoid continuing security policies that were not effective 
 • Target population groups for the acquired company 
 • Country-based restrictions 
 • Tighter controls sensitive data such as dependents, national IDs 

 Best practice 
 Always harmonize. Replicating another platform's security model is not recommended 

 6. Country Configuration and Compliance 
 New countries, statutory fields, data privacy, regulatory reporting 

 Lift and shift 
 Configure acquired countries as stand-alone setups with their own picklists, fields, and templates. 

 Harmonize 
 Align to the parent's country configurations where they already exist. 

 Focus areas 
 • Statutory fields and local labor law requirements 
 • New country setup where the parent has no footprint 
 • Document and contract templates by country 
 • Regulatory reporting continuity (for example EEO and VETS-4212 in the US) 
 • Data privacy requirements such as GDPR 

 Best practice 
 Build a country-by-country readiness checklist with local HR and Legal sign-off. Reuse the parent's configuration where it exists and add only the gaps. 

 7. Historical Data 
 Effective-dated history, archives, retention, right of access 

 Lift and shift 
 Load as much history as the data model allows. 

 Harmonize 
 Load current state record into SuccessFactors 

 Focus areas 
 • Full history should not be converted 
 • Retention policy and who can access the archive after transition 
 • GDPR right of access 
 • Former employees' future needs: tax, immigration, benefits, legal matters 

 Best practice 
 This is often underestimated and surfaces late, usually when a former employee or auditor asks for records that no longer exist in the new system. Define the retention and access model early: where history lives, who can access it, and how former employees can request their records. 

 Part B: Talent Modules 
 8. Performance and Goals Management (PMGM) 
 Goals, review cycles, ratings, calibration, feedback, development plans 
 Performance touches pay, promotion, and how employees feel about being evaluated by a new company. It is also closely scrutinized by works councils. 

 Lift and shift 
 Build separate templates, rating scales, and cycle dates in SF for the acquired population. 

 Harmonize 
 Assign acquired employees to the parent's existing forms, scale, and calendar. 

 Focus areas 
 • Template and permission assignment by population 
 • Rating scale crosswalk (for example 5-point to 4-point or 5-point to 5-point) – determine how past ratings map 
 • Route maps and calibration sessions that include the new group 
 • RBP visibility for ratings and feedback 
 • Performance history of employees 
 • Complete in flight cycle in legacy system 

 Best Practice 
 Honor the in-flight cycle through completion, then onboard the acquired population into the parent's process at the start of the next cycle. Build a rating scale crosswalk and archive historical ratings with controlled access. In Scenario B, skip building a temporary SF process if the parent will not use that module. 

 9. Recruitment and Talent Acquisition 
 Requisitions, candidates, offers, onboarding handoff, compliance reporting 
 Hiring does not pause on go-live day. Open requisitions, in-flight candidates, and offers must continue, and offers are legally sensitive. 

 Lift and shift 
 Create separate requisition templates, approval flows, and offer letter templates for the acquired population. 

 Harmonize 
 Use the parent's templates, workflows, and career site. 

 Focus areas 
 • Requisition and offer approval workflows 
 • Requisition templates tied to job architecture 
 • Onboarding handoff to EC and country-specific fields 

 Best Practice 
 Harmonize while protecting in-flight offers. 
 10. Learning 
 Catalog, curricula, assignments, transcripts, compliance training 

 Lift and shift 
 Migrate the acquired company's courses, curricula, and assignments. 

 Harmonize 
 Move the acquired population into the parent's catalog and assignment model. 

 Focus areas 
 • Completion records and certifications that are compliance-critical 
 • Assignment profiles and exclusion rules, so parent-company mandatory assignments do not flood the acquired population unintentionally 
 • Content licensing 
 • Access for employees and managers 

 Best practice 
 Migrate completion records for compliance-critical items only. Use exclusion rules to control assignments, then phase the acquired population into the parent catalog on a planned schedule. 

 Part C: Operations and Experience 
 These areas keep people paid, informed, and productive from the first day on the new platform. 
 11. Time Off and Work Schedules 
 Leave policies, accruals, balances, holiday calendars, default hours 

 Lift and shift 
 Recreate the acquired policies and accrual rules, and carry over balances. 

 Harmonize 
 Move to the parent's policies. 

 Focus areas 
 • Policy gaps in countries where the parent has no equivalent (manual tracking or a vendor solution) 
 • Work schedule defaults, such as hours defaulting at new hire 
 • Configure work schedules for time off calculations 
 • Holiday calendars by location 

 Best practice 
 Lift and shift at go-live. Changing leave policies mid-transition can create issues. Flag country gaps early and decide on manual or vendor tracking. 

 12. Employee Experience and Language Support 
 Self-service, mobile, documents, language, help desk, communications 

 Lift and shift 
 Provide a separate portal or landing experience for the acquired population. 

 Harmonize 
 Move employees to the parent's portal, mobile app, and support model. 

 Focus areas 
 • Employee and manager self-service readiness 
 • Language support gaps in the UI and translated job aids 
 • Help desk and case routing for the new population 
 • Communications and training before and after cutover 

 Best practice 
 Use the parent's company experience, and close language gaps before go-live. Translated materials also support the works council conversation.

Introduction 
 For an Supply Chain manager, safety stock is never simply “extra stock.” It is a deliberate trade-off between service protection and working capital. Too little buffer creates shortages, backorders, production interruptions and emergency freight. Too much ties up cash while increasing storage, handling, expiry and obsolescence exposure. Inventory-management guidance therefore frames the decision as a balance between carrying cost and the cost of stockouts or backorders. 
 A fixed safety-stock quantity can work when demand is stable. But when requirements rise, fall or shift seasonally, yesterday’s buffer can become either inadequate or excessive. SAP Dynamic Safety Stock addresses this problem by expressing protection as a range of coverage days or periods of requirements rather than relying only on one static quantity. 

 The Operational Problem: A Static Quantity in a Moving Supply Chain 
 Suppose a finished good has a fixed safety stock of 600 units. 
 At demand of 100 units per day, that represents six days of protection. 
 At 200 units per day, the same 600 units represent only three days. 
 When demand later falls to 60 units per day, it becomes ten days of inventory. 
 The master-data quantity has not changed, but its operational meaning has changed dramatically. During the peak, the planner may experience shortage risk. After the peak, the same setting can leave excess inventory. 
 This matters across the full network: 
 At a manufacturing plant , insufficient component buffer can stop production. 
 At a distribution center , insufficient finished-goods buffer can reduce fill rate. 
 For long-lead purchased materials , an understated buffer may not be recoverable before the shortage date. 
 For seasonal or shelf-life-sensitive inventory , an overstated buffer can create ageing and write-off risk. 
 SAP’s own safety-stock material describes the objective as preventing material outages while avoiding unnecessary inventory and overhead. It also recognizes that the appropriate quantity may need to change with time, market conditions and other factors. More broadly, inventory strategy is the classic balance between responsiveness and efficiency: high inventory supports availability, but at higher cost. 
 How SAP Dynamic Safety Stock Works 
 1. Requirements are translated into average daily requirements 
 SAP evaluates requirements over configured planning periods and converts them into an average requirement rate. Depending on the planning setup, those requirements can originate from planned independent requirements, sales orders, dependent requirements or consumption-oriented planning inputs. 
 The coverage profile controls how the average is established, including parameters such as: 
 Period indicator 
 Number of periods 
 Period-length treatment 
 Days per period 
 Minimum, target and maximum range of coverage 
 An operating example of transaction OMIA shows these fields being maintained at plant and coverage-profile level, including weekly periods, the number of periods used for averaging, and minimum, target and maximum coverage values. 
 2. Coverage days are converted into quantities 
 The managerial calculation is straightforward: 
 Dynamic stock quantity = Average daily requirements × Range of coverage in days 
 SAP supports three policy levels: 
 Minimum range of coverage: the lower protection boundary. 
 Target range of coverage: the inventory level toward which replenishment is planned when the lower boundary is breached. 
 Maximum range of coverage: an upper control boundary indicating potential over coverage. 
 Therefore: 
 Minimum stock = ADR × Minimum coverage 
 Target stock = ADR × Target coverage 
 Maximum stock = ADR × Maximum coverage 
 The coverage policy may remain unchanged while the quantities move with requirements. SAP’s published safety-stock material explicitly identifies coverage-profile calculation as one method for creating a dynamic buffer level. 
 3. MRP includes the buffer in net requirements planning 
 MRP nets demand including safety stock against available inventory and planned receipts, then creates supply proposals when required. Operationally, when the projected position violates the lower coverage boundary, the system uses the target level in determining the additional quantity required. 
 The important distinction is that Dynamic Safety Stock influences procurement or production proposals; it does not create physical inventory by itself. The result may appear through planned orders, purchase requisitions or upstream stock-transfer requirements, depending on procurement type and network design. 
 The operational relationship is illustrated below. 

 Figure 1: Operational flow from demand signals through average daily requirements and range-of-coverage parameters into MRP netting, supply proposals, and governance. Release-specific time-dependent safety-stock functionality should be assessed separately from standard coverage-profile logic. 
 A Crucial SAP Terminology and Release Distinction 
 “Dynamic Safety Stock” is sometimes used for several related but not identical capabilities. 
 Classic range-of-coverage logic 
 The long-established ECC approach uses a coverage profile to calculate demand-responsive minimum, target and maximum quantities. SAP’s consulting material describes standard target-range logic as calculating an order-surplus quantity rather than representing a complete future safety-stock time series as separate “real” MRP elements. 
 S/4HANA time-dependent safety stock 
 SAP S/4HANA 2021 documented Time-Dependent Safety Stock within PP-MRP as functionality that makes safety stock more flexible and dynamic. The same release also documented more extensive time-dependent safety-stock methods in the extended planning/PP/DS area, including method determination, period factors, projected safety stock fields and planning-file updates. 
 SAP Consulting Solution DSS 
 SAP’s separate Dynamic Safety Stock Consideration solution can maintain weekly or monthly quantities and create safety-stock requirement and receipt elements that are visible in the stock/requirements list and integrated with MRP and ATP 
 Managerial implication: do not assume ECC coverage profiles, S/4HANA PP-MRP time-dependent safety stock, embedded PP/DS and the SAP Consulting Solution behave identically. Confirm the installed release, planning engine, scope item and licensed add-ons before writing the functional design. 
 Worked Numerical Example 
 Assume the following policy: 
 Planning period: four future periods 
 Minimum coverage: 3 days 
 Target coverage: 5 days 
 Maximum coverage: 7 days 
 Illustrative fixed safety stock for comparison: 600 units 
 No lot-size, rounding or minimum-order constraints in the calculation 

 Planning period 
 Average daily requirements 
 Minimum: 3 days 
 Target: 5 days 
 Maximum: 7 days 

 P1 
 100 
 300 
 500 
 700 

 P2 
 160 
 480 
 800 
 1,120 

 P3 
 80 
 240 
 400 
 560 
 What the inventory manager should see 
 Demand rises from 100 to 160 units per day in P2, so the target rises from 500 to 800 . 
 Demand falls to 80 per day in P3, so the target falls to 400 . 
 A later surge to 220 per day raises the target to 1,100 . 
 The fixed quantity remains 600 throughout: it overprotects P3 but under protects P2 relative to the five-day policy. 

 Figure 2: Illustrative target stock and minimum–maximum corridor generated from the stated assumptions; it is not a guaranteed inventory recommendation. 
 How MRP would respond in P2 
 Suppose the projected available quantity after current requirements and confirmed receipts is 420 units . 
 Minimum boundary = 480 
 Target level = 800 
 Projected stock = 420 
 Illustrative replenishment need before lot sizing: 
 800 - 420 = 380 Units 
 MRP would use the relevant procurement, lot-sizing, rounding, source and scheduling rules when creating the actual proposal. If the projected quantity were 550, it would be above the minimum boundary; the usual range-of-coverage logic would not require replenishment merely to reach the target. 
 Four Practical Use Cases 
 The figures below are illustrative managerial examples, not SAP-delivered defaults or guaranteed business outcomes. 

 Use case 
 Operational trigger 
 Illustrative Dynamic Safety Stock response 
 Expected planning benefit 

 Variable-demand material 
 Daily demand changes from 120 to 180 units; target coverage is four days 
 Target increases from 480 to 720 units 
 Maintains a more consistent protection horizon than a fixed 500-unit buffer 

 Seasonal/volatile demand 
 Forecast rises from 2,000 units per week off-season to 5,000 during peak; target is one week 
 Target rises from 2,000 to 5,000 before peak and falls afterward 
 Supports advance stock build while avoiding a permanently elevated post-season buffer 

 Raw material/component 
 A component’s dependent demand rises from 300 to 500 units per day as finished-goods production increases; target is six days 
 Buffer rises from 1,800 to 3,000 units 
 Provides additional protection against component shortages that could interrupt multiple production orders 

 Finished good/DC inventory 
 A DC forecast increases from 700 to 1,100 cases per day; target is five days 
 Target rises from 3,500 to 5,500 cases; upstream stock-transfer demand can increase accordingly 
 Aligns the DC buffer with the current demand rate and communicates the requirement upstream 
 Where judgment is still necessary 
 A volatile item is not automatically a good candidate. XYZ classification distinguishes relatively stable X items, predictably variable Y items and highly sporadic Z items. For a highly intermittent Z item, multiplying an unstable average by coverage days may create large swings without providing meaningful service protection. Such items may need segmentation, demand cleansing, a statistical method, manual review or a hybrid policy. 
 Dynamic vs. Fixed vs. Judgment Based Safety Stock 

 Decision dimension 
 Dynamic range-of-coverage stock 
 Fixed safety stock 
 Judgment/manual safety stock 

 Responsiveness 
 Quantity changes with calculated requirements 
 Quantity remains constant until changed 
 Changes only when a planner intervenes 

 Maintenance 
 Lower item-level maintenance after profiles are governed 
 Requires periodic mass review 
 High planner effort 

 Planner dependency 
 Moderate: policy and exceptions require oversight 
 Moderate 
 High 

 Inventory exposure 
 Can reduce persistent over coverage when demand falls 
 Can overstock low-demand periods 
 Depends heavily on planner discipline 

 Shortage exposure 
 Can improve alignment when demand rises 
 May become inadequate during peaks 
 May respond well to known events but can be late or inconsistent 

 Scalability 
 Strong for segmented populations 
 Simple but less responsive 
 Weak across thousands of materials 

 Governance need 
 High: profile, horizon, calendar and exception rules 
 Moderate 
 High: rationale, approval and expiry date for overrides 

 Best fit 
 Materials with meaningful and reasonably reliable requirement changes 
 Stable demand, low-value items, simple environments 
 New launches, phase-outs, tenders, one-time events, constrained supply or known changes absent from the forecast 
 Manual judgment should not be eliminated. It should be converted from the default planning method into a controlled exception mechanism . 
 Business Benefits—and the Conditions Behind Them 
 Potential benefits 
 Inventory alignment: Stock quantities can fall when demand falls, reducing persistent excess. 
 Service protection: Buffers can rise when requirements rise rather than waiting for a periodic manual update. 
 Consistent policy language: Managers can discuss “five days of coverage” across materials with different unit volumes. 
 Planner productivity: One governed profile can serve a material segment instead of maintaining every quantity individually. 
 Working-capital visibility: Days-of-supply parameter

items.title: SAP Digital Manufacturing: Can DM-only dispensing order stock be consumed by an ERP process order?
items.author: cothe
items.text:
Hello SAP Community, 
 We are evaluating a pre-weighing and dispensing scenario in SAP Digital Manufacturing integrated with SAP S/4HANA. We would appreciate guidance on whether the following design is supported. 
 Business requirement 
 Raw materials are weighed and divided into containers in a separate dispensing area, then stored and later delivered to production. 
 The material code and batch must remain unchanged after dispensing. 
 Each container must have its own identifier and quantity for traceability. 
 Dispensing must not trigger ERP goods issue or goods receipt. 
 ERP consumption should occur only when the container is actually used in the manufacturing process order. 
 Proposed design — not yet validated 
 Stage raw-material stock from S/4HANA to DM through movement type 311. 
 Use a separate production order in DM to execute dispensing. The order header material is the same raw material being dispensed, and each SFC represents one container. 
 Assemble the original raw-material inventory into the container SFC, reducing the original DM inventory without posting ERP consumption. 
 Complete the SFC to generate container floor stock through internal DM goods receipt, retaining the original material and batch. Prevent ERP postings from this dispensing order. 
 Later, consume the container Inventory ID in an ERP-origin process order using the Material Consumption plugin, triggering movement type 261 in S/4HANA. 
 For example, starting with 100 kg: 
 Stage DM inventory S/4HANA inventory 
 Before dispensing Original stock: 100 kg 100 kg 
 After dispensing 10 kg Original stock: 90 kg; container stock: 10 kg 100 kg 
 After consuming the container in the process order Original stock: 90 kg; container stock: 0 kg 90 kg, with one 261 posting 
 Documentation reviewed 
 Floor Stock Receipt : describes floor-stock generation upon SFC completion. 
 Floor Stock Consumption : describes consumption of transferred, received or generated floor stocks by ERP orders, including process orders. 
 Inventory Management Mode : describes stock creation following production-order SFC completion. 
 KBA 3778100 : explains that DisableGR=true prevents ERP GR replication but does not suppress internal DM goods receipt. We understand that this setting alone does not prevent ERP goods issue. 
 These references describe the individual capabilities, but we have not confirmed the combined scenario above. 
 Questions 
 Is this a supported design, particularly when the dispensing production order has no corresponding order in S/4HANA? 
 Can its generated container stock be selected and consumed by an ERP-origin process order, with the correct 261 posting? 
 What determines the generated stock’s origin, batch and storage location? Can the original raw-material batch be retained? 
 How should integration be configured to prevent ERP GI/GR for dispensing while retaining normal ERP consumption for the process order? 
 Are there restrictions related to inventory management mode or using the same material as both input and output? If this approach is unsuitable, what standard alternative would you recommend? 
 Any relevant SAP Notes, documentation or implementation experience would be appreciated. 
 Thank you.

35.summary: The author creates outbound deliveries with BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CREATE_SLS. FIFO batch determination creates batch-split child items (9000xx) under parent items with LFIMG 0. They need to swap those batches for specific batches scanned on a check sheet, without goods issue. Manually in VL02N this works, but BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CHANGE fails with VLBAPI 004 when changing the child batch, and with /SPE/DIRDLV 006 or 014 when deleting and re-adding child items. The post asks three questions: a supported program path, why the /SPE/ checks run for a storage location without a warehouse number, and whether batch can be passed at creation to skip FIFO. Changing BATCH on the child via BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CHANGE fails with VLBAPI 004 (quantity consistency check).
Deleting the child and adding a new one with HIERARITEM/USEHIERITM fails with /SPE/DIRDLV 006 without STGE_LOC, and /SPE/DIRDLV 014 (no warehouse number for 1000/IFGL) with STGE_LOC.
Add-then-delete attempts show the same errors, and one run committed the delete before the add failed, leaving a parent with no child. This is a data-consistency hazard that the post flags.
The manual VL02N path works, so the failure is specific to the BAPI/program path.
The post asks for a supported way to avoid FIFO at creation time, which would be cleaner than post-hoc item surgery.
technical_details: BAPIs: BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CREATE_SLS, BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CHANGE, BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK.

Structures named: ITEM_DATA (HIERARITEM, USEHIERITM, MATERIAL, BATCH, DLV_QTY), ITEM_ORG (PLANT, STGE_LOC), ITEM_CONTROL (CHG_DELQTY).

35.why_it_matters: Batch changes after determination are common in regulated or serial-controlled flows, and the post shows a real gap between VL02N and the delivery BAPIs. The partial-commit inconsistency is an important warning for anyone writing item-level delivery logic.
35.developer_problem: How can a program replace FIFO-determined batch-split child items in an existing outbound delivery with specific batches, without GUI automation and without posting goods issue?
35.teaching_angle: Good case study for delivery item hierarchy (parent/child batch split), BAPI commit and rollback semantics, and reading BAPI return tables. Ask trainees to explain why a child-item delete plus add can leave an inconsistent parent, and how they would structure a LUW to avoid it. digest.headline: A thin day for core ABAP: a BAPI delivery batch-split failure, a table-to-CDS mapper, a RAP learner series, and a Node.js CVE on BTP.
digest.overview:
Most of today's items are excerpts or unanswered questions, so little is verifiable in depth. The most technical ABAP item is a Q&A on replacing FIFO-assigned batch-split child items in outbound deliveries. BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CHANGE fails with VLBAPI 004 and /SPE/DIRDLV 006/014, and one run committed a delete before the add failed. Also relevant: a new version of a table-to-CDS mapper report (S/4HANA 2025 FPS01), and part 2 of a managed RAP learner series on S/4HANA 2023.

On the platform side, a post claims the BTP nodejs_buildpack still installs vulnerable Node.js versions for CVE-2026-111497, and SAP published AI skills for Neo-to-Application Frontend migration. Several other items show agent and MCP tooling around ABAP (an agent-written set of nine ABAP tools exposed through MCP, an ABAP MCP server catalogue). These raise authorization and commit-control questions the posts do not answer. Treat all claims as unverified until checked against the full source.

top_stories.title: BAPI cannot replace FIFO batch-split child items in outbound delivery
top_stories.summary: A developer creates deliveries with BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CREATE_SLS. FIFO determination creates child items (9000xx) with the batch, and the parent has LFIMG 0. Changing the child batch with BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CHANGE fails with VLBAPI 004. Deleting and re-adding the child fails with /SPE/DIRDLV 006, or 014 when STGE_LOC is passed (storage location IFGL has no warehouse number). VL02N works manually. One run committed the delete before the add failed, leaving a parent with no child. WS_DELIVERY_UPDATE_2 was not tested. No answer is given.
top_stories.why_it_matters: It shows a real gap between the GUI and the delivery BAPIs, and a consistency hazard in item-level delivery changes. Check return tables and roll back before any commit.

deep_dives.title: Safe item-level changes to outbound deliveries with BAPIs
deep_dives.explanation:
The case in ref 35: BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CREATE_SLS with FIFO batch determination produces a parent item with LFIMG 0 and child items (9000xx) carrying the batch. Changing BATCH on the child via BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CHANGE raises VLBAPI 004, a quantity consistency check. Deleting the child and adding a new one with HIERARITEM and USEHIERITM raises /SPE/DIRDLV 006 without STGE_LOC, and 014 when STGE_LOC is passed, because the storage location has no warehouse number.

The main hazard is transactional. One attempt committed the delete before the add failed, leaving a parent without a child. A BAPI that returns errors in RETURN must never be followed by BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT. Check RETURN for types E and A after every call, and call BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK on failure. Do the delete and the add in a single call where the BAPI allows it, so there is one LUW.

WS_DELIVERY_UPDATE_2 with VBPOK_TAB and VBKOK_WA was mentioned but not tested. It may behave differently, so test it in a sandbox. A cleaner design may be to influence batch determination at creation time. Whether the BAPI accepts a batch at creation to skip FIFO is an open question in the post, so verify it in your system rather than assume.

deep_dives.title: From classic table to released CDS view
deep_dives.explanation:
Ref 42 describes a report that starts from a table or field and proposes CDS objects. The excerpt shows no code, so the matching logic is not known. The approach is a direct field relationship, found by looking at which CDS views expose a given table field.

In ADT, you can do something similar by hand. Open the released object tree for the API state, search for CDS views whose data source is the table, and check the release contract (C1 for use in key user and ABAP Cloud, or C0 for extension). The post also lists the Cloudification Repository, which gives successor objects for released/classic objects, and SAP Business Accelerator Hub.

A field match does not mean the CDS view is a semantic replacement. Filters, joins, currency or unit conversion and authorization checks in the view can change the result. Compare row counts and values against the table for a sample before replacing a SELECT in custom code.

deep_dives.title: Managed RAP: validations, determinations, actions and draft
deep_dives.explanation:
Ref 52 is a learner series on managed RAP for S/4HANA 2023. The excerpt lists the features but shows no code, so what follows is general RAP background and not from the post.

In the behavior definition, a validation is declared with the trigger operations and fields, for example validation validateX on save { create; field Y; }, and a determination with determination setDefaults on modify { create; }. Custom actions are declared with action and implemented in the handler class with a MODIFY ENTITIES statement. Draft needs a draft table and the with draft statement, plus the draft actions Edit, Activate, Discard and Resume.

Common problems for learners are validations that fire on the wrong trigger, missing failed and reported entries so messages do not reach the UI, and a missing draft table. A useful teaching step is to have students write each handler method themselves and watch the Fiori Elements behaviour.

interview_questions.question: A BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CHANGE call that swaps a batch-split child item fails after you already deleted the old child. How do you keep the delivery consistent?
interview_questions.answer: Evaluate the RETURN table after every BAPI call and treat types E and A as failure. On failure call BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK and never BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT, so the delete is not persisted. Better, put delete and add in one BAPI call so they share one update, rather than committing between them. Check that the BAPI does not commit internally in your release. In the case reported, a delete was committed before the add failed, leaving a parent with no child. Also consider whether batch can be set at creation, or whether another interface such as WS_DELIVERY_UPDATE_2 is supported. Test any alternative in a sandbox, not production.

interview_questions.question: You must find the released CDS view that replaces direct reads of a classic table, with no successor listed. How do you proceed?
interview_questions.answer: First check the Cloudification Repository for a successor, then the released object tree in ADT and the Business Accelerator Hub. Search CDS views whose data source is the table and which expose the needed fields. Check the release contract (C1 or C0) so the view is allowed in ABAP Cloud or extension use. A field-level match is not proof of equivalence, because the view may add filters, joins, conversions or authorization checks. Compare row counts and values on sample data against the old SELECT. Document the result, and use a mapper report only as a starting point.

interview_questions.question: An agent generates ABAP tools that are exposed to an LLM through an MCP server. What would you review before transporting them?
interview_questions.answer: Check authorization first: each tool should run with the caller's authorizations and use explicit AUTHORITY-CHECK statements, not a technical user with broad rights. Check that write paths do not commit unexpectedly and that commit and rollback are controlled by one owner. Review error handling, so failures return clear messages and do not leave partial updates. Check input validation, because LLM-supplied parameters are untrusted. Run ATC with the clean-core checks and require normal code review and unit tests. Limit the tool list to the read access that is needed, and log tool calls for audit. The post gives none of these details, so this is a review standard, not a description of that project.

class_idea.title: Safe delivery changes with BAPIs: return handling, LUWs and batch split
class_idea.why_now: Today's most technical question (ref 35) shows a BAPI path failing where VL02N works, plus a delete committed before the add failed. A related status BAPI question (ref 36) shows rules that BAPIs enforce.
outline: Delivery item hierarchy: parent, child, HIERARITEM, USEHIERITM
